text: The Palace of Running Waters (Spanish: Palacio de Aguas Corrientes) is an architecturally significant water pumping station located in Buenos Aires, Argentina, and was formerly the headquarters of the state-owned company Obras Sanitarias de la Nación. It is currently administered by Agua y Saneamientos Argentinos (AySA). Designed and completed in the 19th century, the building was commissioned in 1877 by Norwegian architect Olaf Boye, Swedish engineer Carlos Nyströmer, and British civil engineer John Baterman (Bateman, Parsons & Bateman), with construction beginning in 1887 and inauguration in 1894. It was built to replace the unsightly water tower on Lorea Plaza, which is now part of Congressional Plaza, and occupies a city block at the northern end of the Balvanera section along Córdoba Avenue. The structure, a French Renaissance-style palace, is covered with over 300,000 glazed, multi-color terra cotta tiles imported from Royal Doulton, features a tin mansard roof, and displays escutcheons representing the 14 Argentine provinces at the time. It contains twelve water tanks spanning three floors with a total water capacity of 72,000 tons, an iron structure produced in Belgium, and 180 supporting columns. The building was declared a National Historic Monument of Argentina in 1989. Following the 1892 nationalization of the British-owned water company, the palace was transferred to the City of Buenos Aires. In 1978, the water pumps were dismantled and the building was converted into a museum. The company, known as Obras Sanitarias de la Nación (OSN), was reprivatized in 1993 under a 30-year contract, which was rescinded in 2006, transferring the property to AySA. The palace still houses AySA offices, the Historic Archives, and a small water works museum. The entrance is adorned with two caryatids, and the property includes landscaped gardens featuring a bust by Norwegian sculptor Olaf Boye, honoring engineer Guillermo Villanueva, the first director of the Buenos Aires Water Supply and Drainage Company Limited, inaugurated in 1869. Established in 1873, the Historic Archives is the only archive containing complete and specific information about emblematic buildings and water supply planning in Buenos Aires, composed of three main divisions. The building is prominently featured in the book Santa Evita by Tomas Eloy Martinez. Its geographic coordinates are 34°36′02″S 58°23′42″W (34.60056°S 58.39500°W).
